title: The Sufi's donkey
hookLine: dervishes sell a traveler's donkey for a feast, and he joins the chant without knowing what it means (Masnavi 2.514ff)

lines: WARM IN THE MIDDLE OF A CROWD.
cards: Everybody at the concert knows the chorus, so you sing it too, loud, arms up, with no idea what the words are. Everyone at work is sharing the same post, so you share it.
The whole table laughs at a joke you didn't catch, and you laugh harder than anyone. It's warm in the middle of a crowd. It feels like belonging.
Rumi tells a story that is funny right up until the moment it isn't: a traveler, a lodge full of hungry dervishes, and one very unlucky animal.

teach.h: A TRAVELER, A LODGE, A HUNGRY CROWD.
teach.b: It's in Book Two of the Masnavi. A traveling Sufi arrives at a lodge where other Sufis live, the kind of place that takes in wanderers for the night. He leads his donkey into the stable and goes in to join the company.

But the Sufis there are poor, and very hungry. Rumi says they whispered that need can make even forbidden things allowed, and they quietly sold his donkey. With the money they bought food, lit candles and threw a feast.

teach.h: THE DONKEY'S GONE, THE DONKEY'S GONE!
teach.b: After the meal came music and dancing, and the singer started a chant with a catchy refrain: the donkey's gone, the donkey's gone. Everyone joined in, clapping and stamping.
And the guest, full and happy and caught up in it, sang louder than anyone. At dawn, everyone scattered. The traveler went to the stable to load up, and found the stall empty.
He asked the lodge servant what happened. The Sufis sold it, the servant said. Why didn't you come and tell me?
And the servant answered: I did come, several times.

But you were singing the donkey's gone more eagerly than any of them, so I thought you already knew. Rumi has the traveler say that copying them ruined him. Imitation isn't always wrong; we learn a great deal by copying.
But this man sang his own loss because the room was singing. That rounds off our week: the vine, the dyed mind, the shepherd's own words, the obstacle, and now this.
Your line: know what you sing.

how: Readers of Rumi often take this story as a warning against taqlid, blind imitation, and as encouragement to understand the words and practices they take part in.

o: the chant a guest sang about his own lost animal
a Sufi blessing said before a shared feast
a joke about a guest who leaves too early

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: the donkey's gone, the donkey's gone

s: the servant never tried to warn the traveler
he came several times, but the traveler was singing so eagerly he thought he knew.
the traveler sang about his own loss without knowing it
he joined the chant because the whole room was singing.
Rumi says all imitation is wrong
the story warns against copying without understanding, not against learning from others.

games.q: you're the traveler. the room is clapping and chanting 'the donkey's gone!' and everyone is having a wonderful time. what do you do?
o: ask what the song is about.
games.why: he sang the loudest of all, and found out at dawn it was his donkey that was gone.

practice: Let one habit come to mind that you picked up from the people around you: a phrase you say, an opinion you repeat, something you buy, a way you talk about yourself.
Hold it up and ask, gently: do I know what this means, and do I actually agree with it? You don't need to change anything; just know what you're singing.

wordCard.voice: Donkey's gone. The chant the Sufis sang when they'd sold the guest's donkey to pay for their feast, and he sang along without knowing. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian: a donkey. the Sufis' refrain in Rumi's story is 'the donkey is gone'.

carryVoice: Your line: know what you sing. Copying can teach a lot, as long as you know the words. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Masnavi 2.514ff (the Sufi whose donkey was sold)
